# Solution

**Claim.** The only natural number $k$ with the required property is $k=1$.

Let $p_1=2,p_2=3,\dots$ be the primes and $P_k=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ their product (the $k$-th primorial). We seek $k$ such that $P_k-1=n^m$ for natural numbers $n,m$ with $m\ge 2$.

---

## The case $k=1$

$P_1-1=2-1=1=1^2$, which is a perfect power (exponent $2>1$). So $k=1$ works.

---

## The case $k\ge 2$ is impossible

Since $k\ge 2$, the prime $3$ divides $P_k$, so $P_k-1\equiv -1\equiv 2\pmod 3$. Also $P_k$ is even, so $P_k-1$ is odd, hence $n$ is odd.

**Even exponents are impossible.** If $m$ is even, then $n^m\equiv 0$ or $1\pmod 3$ (every square is $0$ or $1$ mod $3$), contradicting $n^m\equiv 2\pmod 3$. Thus $m$ is odd, and $m\ge 3$.

**Reduction to prime exponents.** Write $m=qs$ with $q$ an odd prime. Then $P_k-1=n^m=(n^s)^q$, so $P_k-1$ is a perfect $q$-th power with base $N=n^s\ge 2$ (since $P_k-1\ge P_2-1=5>1$). It suffices to rule out prime exponents, so assume

$$P_k-1=n^q,\qquad q\ \text{odd prime},\ n\ge 2.$$

Then $n^q+1=P_k$. Factor (using that $q$ is odd):

$$P_k=(n+1)\,Q,\qquad Q=\frac{n^q+1}{n+1}=n^{q-1}-n^{q-2}+\cdots-n+1.$$

A standard computation gives $\gcd(n+1,Q)=\gcd(n+1,q)$ (since $Q\equiv q\pmod{n+1}$). Both $n+1$ and $Q$ divide $P_k$, which is **squarefree**, so both are squarefree and their prime factors all lie among $\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$, i.e. are $\le p_k$.

### Case A: $q\le p_k$ (so $q$ is one of the first $k$ primes)

Reducing $n^q\equiv -1\pmod q$ and using Fermat ($n^q\equiv n\pmod q$) gives $n\equiv -1\pmod q$, i.e. $q\mid(n+1)$. Hence $\gcd(n+1,Q)=q$, so $q\mid Q$ as well, and therefore $q^2\mid(n+1)Q=P_k$. This contradicts the squarefreeness of $P_k$ (the prime $q$ occurs only once). ✗

### Case B: $q>p_k$ (so $q$ is **not** among the first $k$ primes)

Every prime divisor of $n+1$ is $\le p_k<q$, so $q\nmid(n+1)$ and $\gcd(n+1,Q)=1$. Thus $n+1$ and $Q$ are coprime, both squarefree, with $(n+1)\cdot Q=P_k$.

Now take any prime $p\mid Q$. Then $p\mid P_k$, so $p\le p_k<q$. Also $n^q\equiv -1\pmod p$, and $p\nmid n$ (else $p\mid n^q$ and $p\mid n^q+1$ forces $p\mid 1$). Moreover $n\not\equiv -1\pmod p$, since $p\mid(n+1)$ would contradict $\gcd(n+1,Q)=1$. Therefore $n^q\equiv -1\not\equiv 1\pmod p$ while $n^{2q}\equiv 1\pmod p$, so the multiplicative order of $n$ modulo $p$ is exactly $2q$. Consequently $2q\mid(p-1)$, giving

$$p\ge 2q+1>q>p_k,$$

contradicting $p\le p_k$. Hence $Q$ has **no** prime divisor, so $Q=1$. But for $n\ge 2$ and $q\ge 3$,

$$Q=\frac{n^q+1}{n+1}\ge\frac{2^3+1}{3}=3>1,$$

a contradiction. ✗

Both cases are impossible, so no $k\ge 2$ satisfies the condition.

---

## Conclusion

Combining both parts, the unique natural number $k$ for which $p_1p_2\cdots p_k-1$ is a perfect power (with exponent greater than $1$) is

$$\boxed{k=1}\qquad(\text{since }2-1=1=1^2).$$

# Solution

**Claim.** The only natural number $k$ with the required property is $k=1$.

Let $p_1=2,p_2=3,\dots$ be the primes and $P_k=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ their product (the $k$-th primorial). We seek $k$ such that $P_k-1=n^m$ for natural numbers $n,m$ with $m\ge 2$.

---

## The case $k=1$

$P_1-1=2-1=1=1^2$, which is a perfect power (exponent $2>1$). So $k=1$ works.

---

## The case $k\ge 2$ is impossible

Since $k\ge 2$, the prime $3$ divides $P_k$, so $P_k-1\equiv -1\equiv 2\pmod 3$. Also $P_k$ is even, so $P_k-1$ is odd, hence $n$ is odd.

**Even exponents are impossible.** If $m$ is even, then $n^m\equiv 0$ or $1\pmod 3$ (every square is $0$ or $1$ mod $3$), contradicting $n^m\equiv 2\pmod 3$. Thus $m$ is odd, and $m\ge 3$.

**Reduction to prime exponents.** Write $m=qs$ with $q$ an odd prime. Then $P_k-1=n^m=(n^s)^q$, so $P_k-1$ is a perfect $q$-th power with base $N=n^s\ge 2$ (since $P_k-1\ge P_2-1=5>1$). It suffices to rule out prime exponents, so assume

$$P_k-1=n^q,\qquad q\ \text{odd prime},\ n\ge 2.$$

Then $n^q+1=P_k$. Factor (using that $q$ is odd):

$$P_k=(n+1)\,Q,\qquad Q=\frac{n^q+1}{n+1}=n^{q-1}-n^{q-2}+\cdots-n+1.$$

A standard computation gives $\gcd(n+1,Q)=\gcd(n+1,q)$ (since $Q\equiv q\pmod{n+1}$). Both $n+1$ and $Q$ divide $P_k$, which is **squarefree**, so both are squarefree and their prime factors all lie among $\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$, i.e. are $\le p_k$.

### Case A: $q\le p_k$ (so $q$ is one of the first $k$ primes)

Reducing $n^q\equiv -1\pmod q$ and using Fermat ($n^q\equiv n\pmod q$) gives $n\equiv -1\pmod q$, i.e. $q\mid(n+1)$. Hence $\gcd(n+1,Q)=q$, so $q\mid Q$ as well, and therefore $q^2\mid(n+1)Q=P_k$. This contradicts the squarefreeness of $P_k$ (the prime $q$ occurs only once). ✗

### Case B: $q>p_k$ (so $q$ is **not** among the first $k$ primes)

Every prime divisor of $n+1$ is $\le p_k<q$, so $q\nmid(n+1)$ and $\gcd(n+1,Q)=1$. Thus $n+1$ and $Q$ are coprime, both squarefree, with $(n+1)\cdot Q=P_k$.

Now take any prime $p\mid Q$. Then $p\mid P_k$, so $p\le p_k<q$. Also $n^q\equiv -1\pmod p$, and $p\nmid n$ (else $p\mid n^q$ and $p\mid n^q+1$ forces $p\mid 1$). Moreover $n\not\equiv -1\pmod p$, since $p\mid(n+1)$ would contradict $\gcd(n+1,Q)=1$. Therefore $n^q\equiv -1\not\equiv 1\pmod p$ while $n^{2q}\equiv 1\pmod p$, so the multiplicative order of $n$ modulo $p$ is exactly $2q$. Consequently $2q\mid(p-1)$, giving

$$p\ge 2q+1>q>p_k,$$

contradicting $p\le p_k$. Hence $Q$ has **no** prime divisor, so $Q=1$. But for $n\ge 2$ and $q\ge 3$,

$$Q=\frac{n^q+1}{n+1}\ge\frac{2^3+1}{3}=3>1,$$

a contradiction. ✗

Both cases are impossible, so no $k\ge 2$ satisfies the condition.

---

## Conclusion

Combining both parts, the unique natural number $k$ for which $p_1p_2\cdots p_k-1$ is a perfect power (with exponent greater than $1$) is

$$\boxed{k=1}\qquad(\text{since }2-1=1=1^2).$$
